title: House of D
full_review:
David Duchovny -- best known for his role on the hit series "The X-Files" -- shows another facet of his talent, as the triple-threat writer, director and star of "House of D" (Lions Gate), a contrived but affecting coming-of-age story.

"House of D" begins in present-day Paris, with expatriate Tom Warshaw (Duchovny) in the midst of a marital crisis with his lovely French wife (Magali Amadei). It's the occasion of their son's 13th birthday, which Tom has missed. His wife's censure prompts Tom to open up about his past, of which he's never spoken.

From that point, the film flashes back to Tom's childhood as a 12-year-old boy (Anton Yelchin) living in 1970s Greenwich Village in New York with his manic, pill-popping, chain-smoking widowed mother (Tea Leoni). It's clear that the bond between mother and son is extraordinarily strong despite her eccentricities. His attachment to her is such that he considers his safest place nestled under her bed with a reading light. Mrs. Warshaw thinks nothing of barging into the bathroom to use the toilet or talk to him when he's taking a shower, much to his embarrassment. (There's nothing kinky here, just a mother who knows no boundaries.)

Tom monitors her intake of pills very carefully, and worries that she might take too many.

His best friend is a mentally challenged adult, Pappass (Robin Williams), the school custodian with whom he shares delivery duties for a local restaurant.

And he's sweet on a pretty schoolmate Melissa (Zelda Williams, Robin's daughter), but has no experience wooing girls at his young age. It happens that he has made friends with an unseen former prostitute whom he calls Lady (Erykah Badu). She speaks to him from her high window at the Women's House of Detention, at that time located in the heart of Greenwich Village. Lady gives him pointers on how to woo Melissa, and even teaches him how to dance for the upcoming school event.

Observing Tom's growing attraction to Melissa, Pappass feels he's losing his buddy, and breaks a store window to steal a bicycle the two of them had been saving up to buy. When Tom takes the rap for his friend's transgression, and gets suspended from school for it, his skittish mother -- fearing the boy's future is ruined -- takes an overdose of sleeping pills. At this point, reader, what follows is a plot spoiler, so don't read on if such things bother you.

Mrs. Warshaw is rushed to the hospital where she remains in a comatose state. Shortly after, Tom comes home to discover unpleasant relatives have moved in and plan to be his caretakers. Learning his mother's vegetative condition is permanent, he rushes to the hospital, quickly unplugs her from the machines that sustain her, and poignantly curls up beneath her bed as at home. The hospital staff rushes in within seconds but apparently are not able to revive her.

Afterward, Tom runs away from home, never to return.

As we know, ending life before its "natural" end is morally wrong. Given the context of this particular story and the character's young age, viewers may take an understanding view of his misguided compassion without justifying it. The action is shown to have serious emotional consequences that haunt him well into adulthood, thus providing the impetus for this character to come back home and make peace with his past, including a healing "reunion" with his mother at her grave. Still, it seems a moral misstep.

Also problematic is the scene where the young Tom is seen snuggling -- fully clothed -- with Melissa on top of a bed, and at one point they go to the restaurant's meat locker to be alone together, but only to hold each other and kiss chastely.

There's also some lame humor involving Tom's French teacher, whose unwitting sexual pronunciation of certain words have the mischievous students in hysterics.

The film has a low-budget feel, and at times seems underlit and visually murky. A glossier presentation, especially given the shamelessly sentimental Hollywood ending, might have been more appropriate, but the 1970s' milieu seems accurately portrayed.

Despite flaws, "House of D" imparts overall admirable messages about the importance of honesty, friendship, filial devotion and the finding of your roots, even if served up in platitudinous doses. ("A boy has to go away before he can come back" is the general tenor.) The mercy killing is another matter, however.

The performances are excellent, especially from young Yelchin but also Duchovny and Frank Langella as the Rev. Duncan, Tom's school principal. Leoni gives a somewhat -- but only slightly -- toned-down version of her manic role in "Spanglish." At first, it's difficult to accept Williams as the simple-minded but wise man-child he plays here, but it's to his credit that we finally accept his impersonation as much as we do.

This film contains tobacco and drug use, some profanity and crude language and expressions, sexual content and innuendo, a suicide attempt, and a problematic euthanasia plot twist. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
